answer.sourceLine: This exact English wording is Fragment CXXIX in George Long’s 1877 translation of Epictetus’s Fragments (preserved in the anthology of Stobaeus), confirmed on both Wikisource and Perseus. Note that the Fragments collected by Stobaeus are of debated authenticity, and the words themselves are Long’s English rendering of a Greek original.

trail: The identical wording appears as Fragment CXXIX in George Long’s 1877 translation on Wikisource.
The same fragment and English text are indexed in the Perseus Digital Library.

Epictetus published nothing himself; the fragments were collected later, chiefly from Stobaeus’s anthology, and few of the ~180 are certainly genuine — this one sits among the doubtful and spurious fragments ↗ in Oldfather’s Loeb edition.

author.heading: About Epictetus
author.metaLine: c. 50 – c. 135 AD · Greek Stoic philosopher, born a slave at Hierapolis
author.bio: Epictetus was a Greek Stoic philosopher born into slavery at Hierapolis in Phrygia (modern Pamukkale, Turkey). After his manumission he taught in Rome until Domitian banished philosophers, then founded a school at Nicopolis in Greece. He wrote nothing himself; his teaching survives through his pupil Arrian’s notes — the Discourses and the Enchiridion — supplemented by later Fragments quoted in the anthology of Stobaeus.

misattribution.heading: Wording & authenticity
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Epictetus is sound, but two honest caveats matter for a quote like this.

items.why: Epictetus taught in Greek and wrote nothing down; this specific English phrasing is George Long’s Victorian rendering, confirmed as Fragment CXXIX on Wikisource. Other translators word it differently.

This line comes from the Fragments gathered mostly from the anthology of Stobaeus, a body of material that scholars flag as being of uneven and sometimes doubtful authenticity, unlike the well-attested Discourses and Enchiridion recorded by Arrian — see the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

misattribution.truthLine: The quote is genuinely printed as Epictetus, Fragment CXXIX, in George Long’s standard 1877 translation — verifiable on Perseus and Wikisource — but remember the words are Long’s English and the fragment tradition is not as secure as the Discourses.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The maxim distills a core Stoic move: happiness is a matter of directing attention. Grief over what we lack is treated as a self-inflicted disturbance, while gratitude for what is already ours is presented as the mark of the wise. It sits comfortably alongside Epictetus’s central teaching in the Enchiridion that some things are within our power and others are not.
context.pull: Rejoice for what you have, rather than grieve for what you have not.
